To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) hydrogen isotopic (δ D) measurements of neoformed clay-rich rocks from the Argentine Puna record the infiltration of meteoric fluid in a fold-and-thrust-belt setting; 2) this fluid was sourced from the surface, and was subsequently reactivated by deformation; and 3) the δD composition of the fluid matches regional Miocene climatic changes.

The main takeaway from our work is that
meteoric fluid infiltration into the upper crust is not restricted to the present-day hydrological cycle.
the source of geothermal fluids is not necessarily deep seated, but can be derived from the surface and infiltrate down into the upper crust.
meteoric fluid infiltration can be an important component of the fluid regime during deformation in orogenic systems, particularly during aridification and glacial periods.
